strengths: The paper addresses a well-defined and challenging gap in online fair division by focusing on PROP1, a natural relaxation of proportionality, which is highly relevant given the strong impossibility results of stronger notions like EF1 and MMS.

The paper provides a comprehensive suite of results, including interesting impossibility results for simple greedy heuristics, a tail bound guarantee for randomized allocation under non-adaptive adversaries, and a learning-augmented algorithm under adaptive adversaries.
The maximum item value (MIV) prediction model is a highly practical and lightweight alternative to the demanding normalization assumptions used in prior work.
The potential-function-based analysis for Theorem 11 is elegant, and the graceful degradation analysis under prediction error is solid and well-explained.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear intuition provided before the technical proofs.
weaknesses: The approximation ratio achieved with perfect MIV predictions is $1/n$, which is quite weak when the number of agents $n$ is large. It remains an open question whether a constant-factor approximation (independent of $n$) is achievable.

The treatment of prediction errors is restricted to one-sided overestimation. While the authors provide reasonable justification for this, in real-world ML systems, two-sided prediction errors (underestimation as well as overestimation) are common, and the paper does not analyze this case.

The paper is entirely theoretical. While theory is the primary focus, a brief empirical evaluation on synthetic or real-world agent preferences would have strengthened the paper by illustrating the actual fairness performance and the behavior of the potential function in practice.

strengths: The paper addresses a very natural and open question in online fair division: the approximability of proportionality up to one good (PROP1).

The introduced prediction model, Maximum Item Value (MIV) predictions, is highly practical, being much more lightweight and realistic than the total valuation normalization assumption used in prior work.

The negative results are comprehensive: they show that three natural greedy strategies fail to guarantee any positive approximation to PROP1 against adaptive adversaries, and that stronger notions like EF1, MMS, and PROPX remain inapproximable even with perfect MIV predictions.
The proposed potential-function-based algorithm (Algorithm 1) is elegant, and its analysis is rigorous, demonstrating a $1/n$-approximation for PROP1 with perfect predictions.

The authors provide a robust transformation (Theorem 12) showing that their algorithm degrades gracefully under one-sided prediction errors, which is well-motivated by practical conservative estimation strategies.
weaknesses: The approximation ratio of $1/n$ achieved with perfect predictions scales inversely with the number of agents, which can be small for large $n$. The paper does not discuss the tightness of this $1/n$ ratio under the MIV model.

The analysis of prediction errors focuses only on one-sided overestimation. In real-world machine learning systems, predictions can be two-sided (i.e., sometimes underestimating), and the performance of the algorithm under underestimation remains unexplored.

The fundamental question of whether a non-trivial PROP1 approximation can be achieved in a purely online setting (without any predictions or randomization) against adaptive adversaries remains unresolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-defined and challenging problem in online fair division, focusing on a highly appropriate fairness relaxation (PROP1) where prior work left a significant gap.

It provides a comprehensive set of results, including negative results for natural greedy algorithms, positive guarantees for randomized algorithms against non-adaptive adversaries, and a novel potential-based algorithm utilizing maximum item value (MIV) predictions.
The proposed algorithm degrades gracefully under one-sided prediction errors, making the learning-augmented analysis robust and practical.
The paper clearly delineates the boundary of what is possible by proving that stronger fairness notions (EF1, MMS, PROPX) remain completely inapproximable even with perfect MIV predictions.
The writing is exceptionally clear, with well-structured definitions, intuitive explanations of the potential functions, and detailed proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: It is currently unclear whether the $1/n$-PROP1 approximation under perfect MIV predictions is tight, or if a constant-factor approximation (independent of $n$) is possible. Discussing upper bounds/impossibility results for approximate PROP1 with MIV predictions would strengthen the work.

The paper lacks a worst-case robustness guarantee for completely arbitrary (or two-sided) prediction errors, although this is understandably due to the open status of the advice-free online PROP1 approximation.
